idiom_name: stdlib small-string form (_SmallString, 15 UTF-8 code units inline) plus inline-layout value types
implementation_notes: Swift realizes the pattern where it matters most: the standard library stores short strings inside the String value itself - _SmallString keeps a (UInt64, UInt64) raw bit pattern with a discriminator bit (isSmall) and a capacity of 15 code units on 64-bit platforms, and the canonical empty string is the zero-sized small string. More generally, structs and enums are value types whose storage is inline wherever they are stored, so a small instance costs no separate allocation at all; heap allocation enters through reference types and the heap-backed containers (Array, Dictionary, and String only once it outgrows the small form). Use the built-in value types and keep small records as structs; write a custom inline buffer only for a payload the standard library does not cover, and prefer stack-scoped scratch APIs (withUnsafeTemporaryAllocation) over an in-object buffer when the storage is temporary.
code_sketch:
let id = "eu-west-1"          // 9 UTF-8 bytes: stored inside the String value
let empty = ""                // the zero-sized small string: no allocation

struct Point { var x, y: Double }   // inline storage wherever it is used

var s = "short"                     // small form: 15 code units available
s += String(repeating: "x", count: 40)   // grows past the buffer -> large form
pitfalls: The small/large distinction is invisible in the type: withUnsafeBufferPointer into a String's UTF-8 storage is valid only inside the closure, because a mutation can switch the string from the small form to a heap form and move the bytes.

Value semantics copy: a struct with a large inline buffer is memcpy'd on every assignment and every capture, and a class instance is always a pointer plus allocation - inline storage only helps types that stay values and are not copied in hot loops.

Copy-on-write containers hide a reference count (Array, Dictionary, String): sharing a value and then mutating it can copy, so a small object held in a shared container may still allocate at the first write.
sources: Swift standard library source, SmallString.swift - _SmallString stores a raw (UInt64, UInt64) bit pattern, with capacity 15 code units on 64-bit platforms and a discriminator byte: https://github.com/swiftlang/swift/blob/main/stdlib/public/core/SmallString.swift

Swift standard library source, StringObject.swift - the bit layout of String, including the isSmall discriminator and the note that small strings 'are just values, always immortal': https://github.com/swiftlang/swift/blob/main/stdlib/public/core/StringObject.swift
